title: Nuclear Reaction Dynamics: Fusion–Evaporation and Superheavy Elements
subtitle: Heavy-ion reactions, from the evaporation residue cross section to the synthesis of superheavy elements, and where my work fits.

figures.alt: Chart of nuclides from curium (Z = 96) up to element 118, with proton number on the vertical axis and neutron number on the horizontal axis. Each known isotope is a coloured cell, and the cells run diagonally upward and to the right, ending at oganesson near neutron number 177.
figures.caption: Chart of nuclides from curium (Z = 96) to element 118, with neutron number on the horizontal axis.
text: Within the Liquid Drop Model, nuclei beyond Z ≈ 104 have no fission barrier and should disintegrate at once. Yet they exist.
Quantum shell corrections add the extra binding energy that stabilises them. The next closed shells are predicted at Z = 114 or 126 and N = 184, the so-called island of stability.
Superheavy elements are not found in nature. They are made artificially, one atom at a time, with heavy-ion accelerators.

sections.heading: The evaporation residue cross section: three steps

steps.title: 1. Capture
steps.text: The projectile and target overcome the Coulomb barrier and the nuclei touch.

steps.title: 2. Formation
steps.text: The touching configuration evolves into a compound nucleus, in competition with quasi-fission.

steps.title: 3. De-excitation (survival)
steps.text: The compound nucleus cools by emitting neutrons and becomes an evaporation residue, in competition with fission.

paragraphs: The evaporation-residue cross section of any fusion–evaporation reaction is the product of one factor for each step. Superheavy elements are its most demanding application.

equations.text: Capture is summed over partial waves ℓ; formation (red) and survival (blue) are the probabilities that follow.

figures.alt: Plot of the compound-nucleus formation probability P_CN, on a logarithmic axis from 10 to the power minus 10 up to 10, against the compound-nucleus proton number Z_CN from 102 to 114, for cold fusion. Six model curves are shown (Adamian et al. 2000, Feng et al., Veselsky, Swiatecki et al., Loveland, and Siwek-Wilczynska et al.). All fall steeply with Z_CN, from about 0.1 near Z = 102 to between about 10 to the power minus 9 and 10 to the power minus 5 near Z = 113, and the curves spread over two to three orders of magnitude.
figures.caption: Formation probability P_CN versus Z_CN for cold fusion, calculated with different models; the models differ by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude.
figures.credit: Figure from R. Naik et al., Phys. Rev. C 76, 054604 (2007).
text: **Capture** can be calculated reliably with optical models and barrier distributions.
**Survival** is treated with statistical models; the key challenge is predicting fission barriers accurately.
**Formation** is the most ambiguous step: published models differ by two to three orders of magnitude. It is the central focus of my work.

sections.heading: The challenges
bullets: **Formation is ambiguous.** Models of the compound-nucleus formation probability disagree by orders of magnitude, and the process is hindered by quasi-fission.
**Cross sections are tiny.** For the heaviest elements they are of the order of picobarns, and predictions for elements 119 and 120 are at the femtobarn level.
**Fission barriers are uncertain.** The survival probability depends strongly on them.
**One atom at a time.** Each event is rare, so every experiment is long and every prediction matters.

sections.heading: How I evaluate the formation probability
paragraphs: I describe formation as a stochastic process, within the fusion-by-diffusion approach. The surface separation s of the two nuclei obeys a one-dimensional Langevin equation, with the system moving over an inverted-parabola barrier of curvature ω under friction β and a random thermal force r(t) at temperature T:

equations.text: Langevin equation with a random force that satisfies the fluctuation-dissipation relation.

Analytical solution: the probability of crossing the inner barrier B. The damping ratio x runs from overdamped (large) to underdamped (small); the second term accounts for the residual kinetic energy, and T′ is an effective temperature.
Overdamped limit used in fusion-by-diffusion: the residual kinetic energy is fully dissipated, and thermal fluctuations alone carry the system over the barrier.

after: **Why one dimension is sufficient.** The surface separation is taken as the slow collective variable. Eliminating the other fast variables, such as the neck, shifts the initial condition of that variable, which is absorbed into a single adjustable parameter, the injection-point distance. The model is therefore deliberately simple and analytical, and its limits are discussed in the manuscript in preparation.
Details: [Fusion dynamics](projects.html#fusion) and [KEWPIE3](projects.html#kewpie3) on the Projects page, and [Publications](publications.html).

sections.heading: Fusion–evaporation reactions: successes so far
paragraphs: Fusion–evaporation reactions have produced elements up to Z = 118 [1]. The measured cross sections follow two patterns:

figures.alt: Plot of measured cold-fusion (one-neutron channel) cross sections in picobarns, on a logarithmic axis from 10 to the power minus 3 up to 10 to the power 7, against the proton number of the compound nucleus from 100 to 120. Points for 208Pb and 209Bi targets with beams from 48Ca to 70Zn fall along a straight line, from about 2.5 times 10 to the power 5 pb at Z = 102 to about 0.02 pb at Z = 113.
figures.caption: Cold fusion (1n channel) with ^208^Pb and ^209^Bi targets: measured cross sections against proton number.
figures.credit: Figure from S. Hofmann et al., Pure Appl. Chem. 92(9), 1387–1446 (2020).
text: **Cold fusion** (^208^Pb and ^209^Bi targets, one-neutron channel): cross sections fall steeply with proton number, from about 10^5^ pb near Z = 102 to about 10^−2^ pb near Z = 113 [1].

figures.alt: Plot of measured hot-fusion (three- and four-neutron channel) cross sections with a 48Ca beam, in picobarns on a logarithmic axis from 10 to the power minus 3 up to 10 to the power 7, against proton number from 100 to 120. Points for 208Pb, 209Bi and 226Ra targets fall steeply to about 15 pb at Z = 108. Points for 238U to 249Cf targets (superheavy nuclei, Z = 112 to 118) lie on a plateau of roughly 0.6 to 10 pb.
figures.caption: Hot fusion (3n and 4n channels) with a ^48^Ca beam: measured cross sections against proton number, with the superheavy nuclei (^238^U to ^249^Cf targets) on a plateau.
figures.credit: Figure from S. Hofmann et al., Pure Appl. Chem. 92(9), 1387–1446 (2020).
text: **Hot fusion** (^48^Ca beams on targets from ^238^U to ^249^Cf, three- and four-neutron channels): cross sections of the order of 1 to 10 pb for the elements from Z = 112 to Z = 118 [1].

sections.heading: Why the model must be refined for new elements
paragraphs: Attempts to synthesise elements 119 and 120 have so far failed. The projectile–target combinations of current experimental interest have predicted cross sections at the femtobarn level.

Predictions of the formation probability differ widely between models, and a simple phenomenological model carries uncertainties that cannot be removed by refitting alone. Refining the formation step, and quantifying its uncertainty, is therefore needed for reliable predictions for new elements.
See the [predicted cross sections for four unmeasured reactions](projects.html#kewpie3) towards Z = 119 and Z = 120.

references: [1] S. Hofmann et al., Pure Appl. Chem. 92(9), 1387–1446 (2020).

[2] R. Naik, W. Loveland, P. Sprunger, A. Vinodkumar, D. Peterson, C. Jiang, S. Zhu, X. Tang, E. Moore and P. Chowdhury, “Measurement of the fusion probability P_CN for the reaction of ^50^Ti with ^208^Pb”, Phys. Rev. C 76(5), 054604 (2007).
intro: Fusion–evaporation reactions and the synthesis of superheavy elements are parts of one subject, nuclear reaction dynamics, described by the same three-step factorisation of the evaporation residue cross section. Production cross sections for superheavy nuclei, including Z = 119 and Z = 120, are predicted with the KEWPIE2 and KEWPIE3 framework, and the work connects to experimental studies of synthesis and decay at S^3^.
